text: Everything in this chapter so far has been conceptual. This lesson is the applied version: how to actually read a real published device connectivity map, the kind every provider console shows you, and use it to make a real decision about which physical qubits to run a circuit on.

Providers like IBM Quantum publish a visual map for each backend: a node for every physical qubit, laid out to match the chip's real topology — heavy-hex, grid, whatever the device uses — with edges drawn between qubits that support a direct two-qubit gate. That's the connectivity graph from earlier in this chapter, made concrete for one real piece of hardware. These maps aren't static wiring diagrams — they're usually overlaid with live or recent calibration data, so the nodes and edges are colored or labeled with real, measured numbers.

Each qubit node carries its own measured numbers — single-qubit gate error, readout error, T1 and T2 from Chapter 1 — and each edge carries its own two-qubit gate error, measured specifically for that pair. This per-edge detail matters: two edges that look identical in the topology diagram can have measurably different real error rates, often by a factor of two or more, because of manufacturing variation and local calibration drift, which Chapter 5 covers in depth. This is telling you, concretely, how this specific pair of qubits currently performs — not an average, not a spec-sheet number, usually updated daily.

A practical reading checklist: first, confirm your circuit's required interactions are actually coverable by the device's topology, or identify where SWAPs will be unavoidable. Second, scan for the region of the chip with the lowest two-qubit edge errors and best readout and coherence numbers — a sweet spot. Third, check whether that sweet-spot region happens to match the connectivity pattern your circuit actually needs, since a low-error region that doesn't fit your circuit may help less than a slightly higher-error region that does. That tension, error quality versus connectivity fit, is usually the real decision — and only the live device map can answer it.

That closes out connectivity and topology. Next chapter: the classical half of every quantum computer — the wall of ordinary electronics doing almost all of the physical work of generating, routing, and reading the signals a handful of qubits actually respond to.
